vignette:
He remembers the exact sound of the beep. Not the monitor's normal rhythm-the one that stayed steady for three weeks in the PICU-but the sudden flatline tone that ripped through the 3 a.m. silence. That was six years ago. His daughter, Mira, was four. She had been a healthy, giggling child until a sudden fever turned into sepsis, then multiple organ failure. He can still feel the cold vinyl of the hospital chair pressing into his back, the way his wife's nails dug into his palm, the way his own voice sounded foreign when he screamed for a nurse. They coded her twice that night. She survived. He didn't.

These days, Ravi works from the small studio he built in the garage. He is a character animator for a streaming network, known for his fluid, whimsical movements-cartoon animals that bounce and dance. But since Mira's illness, his hand has tightened. He draws scenes of hospitals, waiting rooms, IV poles, but always erases them before anyone sees. When a director sends a storyboard with a sick child, even a minor background element, Ravi's chest tightens. He finds a reason to reject the assignment: the deadline is too short, the rig is too complex. He doesn't say why. He cannot say why.

At home, he checks on Mira's breathing every night. She is ten now, healthy and strong, running through the backyard with her friends. But Ravi still stands in her doorway at 2 a.m., watching the rise and fall of her chest. He times each breath. If she shifts in her sleep, his stomach drops. He once drove her to the emergency room because she coughed twice in a row. The doctor said it was allergies. Ravi didn't sleep for two days.

His wife, Priya, has stopped asking why he sleeps on the couch. She knows about the nightmares-Mira's face turning blue, the beep, the doctors saying "we're losing her"-but she doesn't understand why he won't talk about it. When she tries to bring up that night, Ravi's jaw locks. He stares at a fixed point on the wall. His mind goes blank, or full, he can't tell. He just knows the pressure in his chest is unbearable, and the only way to stop it is to leave the room. He goes to his studio and animates a single looping sequence: a butterfly landing on a flower, again and again, for hours.

At work meetings, he is sharp. He notices every detail-a dropped coffee lid, a flickering light, a colleague's hand tremor. These details lodge in his mind like splinters. He cannot stop tracking them. He has constructed elaborate mental escape routes for every room he enters. He keeps his back to the wall in restaurants. He avoids hospitals entirely, even for his own checkups. Once, when his mother-in-law was admitted for a minor surgery, he drove her to the entrance and said he had a deadline. He waited in the parking lot for four hours, shaking, gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened.

Last week, his supervisor asked him to lead a short film about a child's first day at school. Ravi said no. He gave no reason. He feels the old tightness climbing up his throat now, just thinking about it. He hasn't cried since the night Mira coded. He doesn't trust himself to start.

He sits in his studio, cursor blinking on an empty canvas. He wants to draw a laughing child. He cannot. The beep is still in his ears.
